title: Comments of the Idaho Office of Species, Minerals, & Energy Coordination et al. encouraging FERC to ensure broader framework reflects the diversity etc. re the Interconnection of Large Loads to the Interstate Transmission System under RM26-4.

            October 7, 2026

            Debbie-Anne Reese
            Federal Energy Regulatory Commission
            Secretary of the Commission
            888 First Street, NE
            Washington, DC 20426

            Re: Interconnection of Large Loads to the Interstate Transmission System, Docket No. RM26-4-
            000

            Dear Ms. Reese:

                    The undersigned western state energy offices appreciate the Federal Energy Regulatory
            Commission's (“FERC” or “the Commission”) efforts to address the complex challenges
            associated with integrating large electric loads into the nation's transmission system. States
            across the West are experiencing unprecedented interest from data centers and supporting
            infrastructure, advanced manufacturing facilities, mineral processing operations, and other
            energy-intensive industries. The scale, concentration, speed, and operation of many of these
            loads distinguishes current growth from the incremental demand growth existing processes were
            designed around. Ensuring that these customers can be served in a timely, transparent, and
            reliable manner is increasingly important to our states' economic development and energy
            planning efforts.

                    We commend the Commission for recognizing that existing transmission service and
            planning processes must evolve to accommodate rapid load growth. We note, however, that the
            Commission's recent action focuses primarily on Regional Transmission Organizations (RTOs)
            and Independent System Operators (ISOs). Many of the same issues identified by the
            Commission are also emerging in regions served by vertically integrated utilities and other non-
            organized market structures, though they arise under different regulatory frameworks. We
            appreciate the Commission's recognition that public utilities and states outside organized markets
            should participate in this discussion. As Chairman Laura Swett noted, transmission providers and
            other stakeholders outside RTO and ISO regions are encouraged to address these issues through
            individual filings.

                   The western United States includes a diverse mix of investor-owned utilities, public power
            systems, generation and transmission cooperatives, and federal transmission providers. Most
            operate outside organized RTOs and ISOs and have unique planning and regulatory structures.
            Reforms developed for RTOs and ISOs may not translate directly to non-RTO regions.
            Nevertheless, they face the same fundamental challenges identified by the Commission: rapidly
            increasing requests for large electric service, pressure to accelerate infrastructure development,

            the need for transparent and faster study processes, and the responsibility to protect existing
            customers while maintaining reliable electric service.

                    As the Commission considers next steps in this proceeding, we respectfully encourage
            FERC to ensure that any broader framework reflects the diversity of utility structures across the
            country. Large-load growth is a national issue, not one confined to organized wholesale markets.
            Principles explored in this proceeding, such as reforms related to transmission service application
            and study processes, cost allocation and cost-shift protections, co-location and behind-the-meter
            generation, new transmission services for flexible loads, and treatment of proximate or co-located
            generation, may provide useful guidance for all jurisdictional utilities while preserving flexibility for
            differing state regulatory frameworks and processes.

                   Timely access to electric service has become a critical component of economic
            development. Speed in one portion of development provides limited value if a project remains
            delayed by disconnected decisions elsewhere. Businesses evaluating locations for major
            investments increasingly prioritize certainty regarding study timelines, infrastructure
            requirements, and expected service dates. While the Commission has highlighted these
            challenges within organized markets, many non-RTO utilities employ transmission service
            processes that differ from those used in organized markets and may benefit from continued
            dialogue regarding transparency, predictability, and best practices.

                    We encourage the Commission to continue engaging with non-RTO utilities and states,
            including through additional guidance or stakeholder forums that support utilities choosing to
            evaluate their existing practices.

                     Finally, as the Commission evaluates potential reforms, we urge the preservation of the
            longstanding balance between federal and state authority. States retain primary responsibility for
            retail electric service, utility regulation, development policies, integrated resource planning, and
            economic development. Federal reforms should respect these jurisdictional boundaries while
            promoting efficient transmission service and prudent infrastructure investment, close coordination
            will be necessary to ensure reforms are effective.

                    As the Commission develops national policy around large load growth, western states
            welcome continued opportunities to share our perspectives so that future federal actions
            recognize the diversity of utility structures, preserve state authority, and provide flexibility for
            differing regional circumstances.
